opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I should be careful here. A private conversation is a private conversation, and I don't want to put words in Ilya's mouth or pretend I know SSI's internal roadmap. Nobody outside really does, and that's partly by design. So I'll only tell you what I took away from it, my own interpretation.

The strongest impression was that he really believes the current paradigm isn't the end of the story. For several years, scaling pre-training was the recipe: more data, more compute, bigger models, and it worked remarkably well. But I think he sees that era as reaching a different phase. The internet's text is finite, and simply turning the same knob doesn't give you the same returns. So the question becomes: what is the next thing to scale? What's the missing ingredient?

From my perspective, a lot of it comes back to generalization. These models can be extraordinary on benchmarks and still fail in ways a human never would. They need enormous amounts of data to learn things a child picks up from very little. That gap between what the models do on evaluations and how robustly they actually understand the world is, I think, something he takes very seriously as a research problem, not an engineering problem. It's not "build a bigger cluster." It's "we don't fully understand something fundamental about learning yet."

That resonates with me a lot, because it's close to why I care about vision and world models. Language is an incredibly compressed, human-curated signal, but it's not the world. If you want systems that learn efficiently and generalize, I suspect you need them grounded in something richer: perception, interaction, the structure of the physical world. I'm not claiming that's SSI's direction. That's my bias, and I told him as much. But we found real common ground in thinking that the next breakthroughs will look more like new ideas than bigger versions of old ones.

The other thing I respect is the focus. The "straight shot" framing, one goal, no product distractions, is unusual right now. Most labs are pulled in a hundred directions by commercial pressure. Whether that bet pays off, nobody knows. But as a researcher, I find it refreshing that someone is saying: let's go back to the age of research, think hard, and try to get the fundamentals right, including safety, rather than treating it as an afterthought.

So my honest summary is that I don't know exactly what they're building. But I understood the spirit of it: the bottleneck is now ideas, not just scale, and generalization is at the heart of it.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute to Ilya a view that general perceptual modeling is already well solved. It instead describes generalization as an unresolved problem and mentions perception as a possible grounding for future systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I have to be careful here, because Ilya is very protective about what SSI is doing, and I don't think it's my place to reveal anything he said in private. But I can share how I understand it at a high level, from the conversation and from what he's said publicly.

The first thing that struck me is that he genuinely believes the current paradigm—scaling pre-training on internet text—has a ceiling. Not that it stops working, but that the marginal returns are changing, and more importantly, that it's not the path to the kind of intelligence he cares about. He said something like, data is the fossil fuel of AI. We only have one internet. And once you've consumed it, you have to find a different way to generate signal.

So the question SSI is asking is not "how do we build a better product" or "how do we get to the next benchmark." It's closer to: what is the actual mechanism of learning that would let a system become superintelligent, and how do you make that safe from the very beginning rather than bolting safety on afterward. The name is very literal. Safe superintelligence. One goal, one product, no intermediate commercial pressure. He was quite explicit that he thinks the race dynamics in the industry right now are distorting research priorities, and that a lab insulated from that could think on a different time horizon.

What I found interesting as someone who works on vision and multimodal models is that Ilya thinks much more from first principles than most people I talk to. He's not interested in incremental architecture tweaks. He's asking things like: what does it mean for a model to generalize? Why do humans learn from so few examples? What would it take for a system to really understand the world rather than imitate text about it? Those are the questions I'm obsessed with too, just coming from the visual side. So we actually agreed on a lot—that current models are still fundamentally impoverished in how they perceive and ground things, and that fixing that is not just a matter of adding more tokens.

I'd say my reading is that SSI is making a bet on finding a new paradigm, something beyond next-token prediction scaling, and doing it quietly. Whether that's a different objective, a different way of generating data, a different notion of reasoning—I'll leave that to him. But what I took away is that he's one of the few people who is both willing to say the current approach is not enough and willing to actually go spend years looking for what's next. That's rare. Most people say the first part and then keep scaling anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says current models are fundamentally impoverished in perception and grounding and that this needs to be fixed. It does not attribute to Ilya the view that general perceptual modeling is already solved quite well.

astra-6.text:
My impression is that SSI is organized around a very focused question: how do you get to safe superintelligence? That’s a different starting point from building a product and letting research follow the product roadmap. It gives you room to pursue ideas that may take longer to validate.

But I’d distinguish that broad ambition from a specific technical direction. I don’t have enough visibility to say what architecture or training approach they’re betting on, and I wouldn’t want to turn an impression from a conversation into a claim about their research plan. The interesting question for me is how safety shapes the research itself—what you optimize for and how you judge progress as the system becomes more capable.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses SSI’s focus on safe superintelligence but does not attribute to Ilya a view about general perceptual modeling being solved.
